chunks: "A differential probe measures the voltage between two points, not a point relative to ground.
It has two inputs, plus and minus, and an amplifier that outputs the difference to the scope, while rejecting whatever voltage they both share.
That shared part is the common-mode voltage, and how well it is rejected is the CMRR. I'd need one any time neither side of what I'm measuring is at ground.
The classic example is the gate drive of a high-side MOSFET in a half-bridge: the source is the switch node, jumping from 0 to, say, 400 volts every cycle.
If I clipped a normal probe ground there I'd short the switch node to earth through the scope.
Other cases are a shunt on the high side of a rail, measuring across a floating sensor, or looking at the two lines of a differential pair directly.
Also anywhere I'm worried about a ground loop corrupting a small signal.
The cautions: CMRR drops with frequency, so a probe that has 80 decibels at DC may give only 30 or 40 decibels at 100 megahertz.
It's more expensive and noisier than a passive probe and has a limited input range. For very high voltage or fast edges, like GaN or SiC, I'd look at an optically isolated probe."
